extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, instrument-makers, assayers, miners, physicians, and practical agriculturists (readers of the Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and criteria for constructing, calibrating, and using an immersion/ballast instrument to test coins and estimate metal fineness, plus related observational and experimental methods in natural philosophy (optics, microscopy, zoology, horticulture, mining).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The instrument's ball (float) should contain as much air as will keep the whole instrument, when loaded, from sinking beneath the top of the stem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the internal cavity size relative to plate thickness so the instrument remains erect and steady in the water when loaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stem attachment and form
rubrics_metrics.description: The stem is soldered to the ball at the uppermost hole; it may be hollow or solid but should be very slender and not too short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make stem slender so different depressions in the water are more notable; if used for other purposes than examining guineas, avoid making it too short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin-holder (screw/stirrup) design
rubrics_metrics.description: At the undermost hole insert and solder a short brass screw or stirrup with a broad slit to receive the edge of the guinea; the stirrup G may be a bent wire standing horizontally to lay the guinea on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide means to fasten the coin by turning the screw one or two turns; ensure holders also support thin plates when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detachable undermost stem and ballast plates
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the undermost stem and the screw removable so they can be thrust on or off the stem to add or remove ballast plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flat round plates with a central hole fitting the stem so one can put on one, two, or three for ballast and then thrust the screw on after them; this allows adjustment of weight for different coins or to support thin plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration using a known genuine coin (marking H)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hang a known genuine coin at the bottom, stop the orifice of the stem, immerse perpendicularly nearly to the top of the stem, let settle, and if it remains make a mark (H) where the water surface touches the stem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the instrument emerges, add weight (in stem or via ballast); if it sinks, reduce ballast by filing or removing weight; once settled, mark the water level as the reference for genuine coin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary calibration using a brass plate (marking I)
rubrics_metrics.description: After marking with the genuine coin, substitute a small round brass plate of the same weight (or a grain or two heavier) and immerse; when it settles make another mark (I) at the water-stem intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two marks allow comparison of candidate coins against a known standard weight and a standard substitute to detect differences in buoyancy/fineness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting ballast when instrument floats or sinks
rubrics_metrics.description: If the instrument emerges too much, add a little weight (shot, filings, or ballast plates); if it sinks beneath water, make it lighter by filing or scraping off some ballast plate or removing some internal weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust iteratively until the instrument with standard load sits at desired mark; ballast should be removable and tunable for fine adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting washed coins versus impure alloy (use of balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a suspected coin is too light in water but has its due weight in air, this suggests it has been made too light by washing (removal of substance) rather than impurity of fineness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve doubts by weighing the suspect coin in the air and comparing to its expected air weight; discrepancy patterns indicate washing versus alloying.

rubrics_metrics.name: General quantitative detectability method (weighing in air and water)
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide whether a particular instrument will distinguish two coins/metals: weigh the piece in air and in water and subtract to get lost weight; do likewise for the likely counterfeit metal (e.g., copper/brass); subtract the smaller difference from the greater to get the remainder which shows how much the true coin will outweigh the other in water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adding that remainder in grains to the lighter metal makes it depress the instrument to the genuine mark, then the instrument can probably discover the difference; recommend having several instruments adjusted for different coin sorts for frequent examinings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using immersion instrument to distinguish pure tin and adulterated tin
rubrics_metrics.description: Because tin is the lightest metal known, if two pieces have the same air weight the adulterated one (mixed with heavier metal) will sink lower than pure tin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare depressions in the instrument for equal air-weight samples; greater depression indicates heavier alloying metal present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pewter composition estimation by comparative depression
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe how much the instrument is depressed by a piece of pewter known to be good; then load with an equally heavy sample under examination—if it sinks deeper it indicates a greater proportion of lead in the mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small standard masses (drams or ounces) of known pewter composition as calibrants for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating gold fineness with calibrated mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Fit the instrument to sink to the tip of the pipe with a determinate weight of the finest gold (24 carats) of an air weight conveniently divisible; make mixtures with known proportions of silver and gold and mark where the water surface cuts the stem for each mixture to observe decreasing depression as silver proportion increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed with as many mixtures/degrees of alloy as convenient and always keep the air weight equal to that of pure gold; use the resulting marks to interpolate fineness of unknown pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending the method to silver, solders, bell-metal, and other alloys
rubrics_metrics.description: By the same method (adjusted appropriately) one may examine different allays of pure silver with copper or lighter metals, estimate how much various coins are debased, assess tin added to copper for bell-metal, and estimate proportions in solders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust instrument scale (e.g., to an ounce of pure copper) and use mixtures of known composition to produce calibration marks for later comparisons; claims this may be nearer truth than touchstone and cheaper than other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly practice: provide numbers and proper attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing astronomical or theoretical systems, adorn them with numbers and explanations fit for trial; acknowledge original authorship rather than representing another's system as your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print full numerical data and explanations so others can test the hypotheses; cite and credit the proper inventor to avoid injustice and to enable verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precise timed astronomical observations for longitude difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Record precise timings (penumbra, umbra, total immersion) of lunar eclipses (and timings of satellite eclipses) at different locations to determine the difference of longitude between places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide careful time-of-contact observations and compare datasets from different observatories to deduce meridian differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopical preparation and observation (optic nerve, blood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dry an optic nerve, make transverse sections and observe structures (holes resembling a leathern sieve); observe sanguineous globules and note that their firmness/pliability changes with the observer's bodily state and may relate to health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful sectioning and drying techniques; relate observed microscopical forms (globule shape/elasticity, quadrangular saline figures) to physiological conditions as hypotheses to be tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical assertions on rainbow formation (numbered propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of propositions explaining rainbow formation: each illuminated raindrop emits a complete rainbow after two refractions and one reflection; rays emerge coloured (red, yellow, green, blue, purple); there are two rings per drop with specific angular relations (one ~21°, the other ~78° from axis); only certain incident rays (angles between ~45° and ~75°) contribute; green arises from mixture of yellow and blue; different parts of solar limb produce different colours; many rainbows exist simultaneously (one per spectator) and a spectator sees a different rainbow at each moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numbered assertions (1–13) specify geometric/optical conditions and angular ranges that constitute the explanatory framework; they are to be judged by how well observations (angles, colours, multiplicity) match the propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification, signs, and remedies for four mine 'damps'
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify four sorts of damp in caverns/mines: (1) ordinary damp—signs: candles burn orbicularly, flame lessens, shortness of breath; remedy: lay person on belly in hole, give ale if necessary; (2) pease-bloom damp—smells like pease-bloom, summer occurrence, usually not mortal; (3) pestilential damp—visible round film/ball on vault that disperses when broken and suffocates; remedy: break at distance and purify by fire before re-entering; (4) explosive vapour—ignited by candle producing report and lightning-like effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize damp type by sensory signs and take corresponding precautions (avoid, break at distance, purge by fire, rescue procedures) as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and explanation of 'fairy-rings' and vegetation anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairy-rings (bare/brown rings or verdant peripheral rings) can be caused by the growth of agaricus fungi or by lightning burning a circular border; digging 2 inches reveals fungus spawn in bare rings but not in revived green rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct ground inspection (digging small depth) and historical observation (post-thunder occurrence) to distinguish fungal from lightning causes; observe regrowth patterns in following seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural observations on manuring and soil
rubrics_metrics.description: Seaweed as manure greatly increases barley yields but tends to produce poorer oats and thicker husks; some sandy soils manured only with seaweed yield extraordinary crops (16–18 fold); some patches produce abundant barley without any manure, possibly due to subterraneous exhalations or washed-down materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation across years, noting crop type response (barley vs oats) and soil characteristics; do not assume a single cause—investigate local factors like exhalations or runoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical/curative observation for vermicular vomiting in infants and children
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases of violent vomiting in infants/children may expel active hexapodes or worms after administration of wormwood ale or powders containing mercurius dulcis; collected expelled specimens should be examined (alive/dead) and tested for feeding and life-cycle behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record treatment, specimen recovery, vivisection or feeding experiments, and preservation methods (e.g., spirit of wine) to study the organisms and link them to clinical recovery.
